prompt: A session ran `BEGIN; SELECT count(*) FROM orders_live;` and the SELECT has returned. When does it release its lock on the table?
hint: psql's prompt still shows a star.

choices.text: At COMMIT or ROLLBACK
choices.why: Right. A lock lasts until the end of the transaction, not the end of the statement.

choices.text: As soon as the SELECT returned its rows
choices.why: That is the belief that makes an idle transaction look harmless. pg_locks still showed it granted.

choices.text: After deadlock_timeout, one second later
choices.why: deadlock_timeout is when PostgreSQL checks for a deadlock; it releases nothing.

choices.text: When another session asks for a conflicting lock
choices.why: Asking does not take it away. The ALTER waited until the COMMIT.

prompt: In the capture, the third session's `SELECT status …` had `blocked_by` = the ALTER's pid, not the first session's. Why?
hint: Which granted or queued lock does an ACCESS SHARE conflict with?

choices.text: Because pg_blocking_pids only ever reports the most recent session
choices.why: It reports every process that blocks; the ALTER's row named the first session.

choices.text: The first session had already committed by then
choices.why: It was idle in transaction with its lock granted, as the same query showed.

choices.text: A SELECT always waits for any ALTER on the same database, whatever the table
choices.why: Locks here are per table. Other tables were not affected.

choices.text: Its lock conflicts with the ACCESS EXCLUSIVE queued ahead of it
choices.why: Right. Two ACCESS SHARE locks coexist; the queued ALTER is what stands in the way.

prompt: In pg_stat_activity, a session that opened a transaction and is waiting for its client to send the next command has the state `idle in ___`.
hint: Three words in the state; the last is missing.

prompt: A colleague adds a nullable column with no default to a busy table at noon. It is instant on their test copy. On production, the site stops answering for three minutes. Which explanation fits this lesson?
hint: What was different on production that the copy did not have?

choices.text: The column made PostgreSQL rewrite the table
choices.why: A column with no default only edits the catalogue, on production as on the copy.

choices.text: A transaction held the table for three minutes, and every query queued behind the waiting ALTER
choices.why: Right. The ALTER itself took milliseconds once it got its lock.

choices.text: Production has more rows, and the time grows with the row count
choices.why: For this change the time does not depend on the number of rows.

choices.text: max_connections was too low
choices.why: Running out of connections is a consequence of the queue, not its cause.

prompt: With `SET lock_timeout = '2s'`, what happened to the ALTER while the first session held the table?
hint: Read its Time: line.

choices.text: It waited two seconds and then ran anyway
choices.why: It did not run; the column source was only added later, by the retry script.

choices.text: It cancelled the first session's transaction so it could proceed
choices.why: lock_timeout only affects the session that set it. The first session committed normally.

choices.text: It gave up after two seconds with an error
choices.why: Right: canceling statement due to lock timeout, and the queue behind it moved.

choices.text: It ran in the background and finished when the lock was free
choices.why: PostgreSQL has no background ALTER. A statement either waits or gives up.

prompt: A change rewrites a large table and needs about a minute of work. Which setting lets it run but stops it from queueing for long?
hint: One counts waiting for a lock, the other counts everything.

choices.text: statement_timeout = '2s'
choices.why: That counts the whole statement, work included, so it would cancel the rewrite after two seconds.

choices.text: idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '2s'
choices.why: That ends sessions sitting idle inside a transaction, which helps, but it limits other people's sessions, not the ALTER's wait.

choices.text: deadlock_timeout = '2s'
choices.why: That is how long to wait before checking for a deadlock. A queue is not a deadlock.

choices.text: lock_timeout = '2s'
choices.why: Right. It counts only the wait for the lock; the minute of work is not limited.

prompt: In the lock_timeout demonstration, the third session's SELECT reported about 1.2 seconds. Why was it not instant?
hint: lock_timeout limits a queue; does it prevent one?

choices.text: Reading a million rows to find id 1 takes that long on any machine, lock or no lock
choices.why: The same query took a fraction of that once nothing was queued; most of the time was waiting.

choices.text: It queued behind the ALTER until the ALTER gave up
choices.why: Right. The queue still formed, and lock_timeout bounded how long it lasted.

choices.text: It had to wait for the first session to commit
choices.why: The first session committed after the SELECT returned; it never blocked the SELECT directly.

choices.text: Its own lock_timeout made it wait two seconds first
choices.why: Only the second session set lock_timeout, and the setting is a ceiling on waiting, not a delay.

prompt: In retry-ddl.sh, why does the script sleep for three seconds between attempts, longer than the two seconds each attempt may wait?
hint: What happens to the queries that were stuck behind the ALTER?

choices.text: PostgreSQL refuses a second ALTER within three seconds of a failed one
choices.why: There is no such rule. Retrying at once would work, and would queue everybody again at once.

choices.text: To give autovacuum time to finish the table
choices.why: The holder here was a transaction, not autovacuum, and three seconds would not finish a vacuum anyway.

choices.text: So the queued queries run, and the holder may finish, before it queues again
choices.why: Right. The gap is the application's time to breathe between attempts.

choices.text: psql needs time to close its previous connection
choices.why: Each psql exits completely before the next line of the script runs.

prompt: On PostgreSQL 16, `ALTER TABLE orders_live ADD COLUMN channel text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'web'` took milliseconds on a million rows. Why?
hint: Where does the 'web' of an old row come from?

choices.text: NOT NULL columns are filled in later, a page at a time, by autovacuum running in the background
choices.why: Autovacuum never writes column values. The catalogue supplies them.

choices.text: The default is kept in the catalogue and supplied when old rows are read
choices.why: Right, since version 11. The file kept its name: no rewrite.

choices.text: Text columns take no space
choices.why: They do, when a value is stored. Here nothing was stored in the rows.

choices.text: Because the table had no indexes yet
choices.why: A rewrite without indexes still copies every row; the volatile default proved it on the same table.

prompt: Match each change to orders_live with what it cost.
hint: Look at the file name and the DEBUG lines.

pairs.left: ADD COLUMN token uuid DEFAULT gen_random_uuid()
pairs.right: A rewrite: every row gets its own value

pairs.left: ALTER COLUMN status TYPE varchar(40), from varchar(20)

pairs.right: A rewrite: every row changes size

right_distractors: A rebuild of every index on the table

prompt: How did the lesson tell, without timing anything, that ALTER COLUMN total_cents TYPE bigint rewrote the table?
hint: Two signs, one a function from lesson 4.

choices.text: pg_locks showed ShareUpdateExclusiveLock
choices.why: It showed AccessExclusiveLock; ShareUpdateExclusiveLock was VALIDATE's lock.

choices.text: The number of rows reported by the ALTER
choices.why: ALTER TABLE reports no row count, rewrite or not.

choices.text: The table's size in \dt+ doubled and stayed doubled until the next VACUUM FULL ran
choices.why: A rewrite replaces the file; the old one is removed when the transaction ends.

choices.text: pg_relation_filepath changed, and DEBUG1 said rewriting table
choices.why: Right. A rewrite is a new file, and PostgreSQL says so at debug1.

prompt: A migration file runs ten ALTER TABLE statements inside one BEGIN … COMMIT, on ten different tables. The first one rewrites a large table. What does that mean for the other nine tables during the migration?
hint: When are locks released?

choices.text: Each table is locked only while its own ALTER runs
choices.why: Each lock is taken when its ALTER runs, and released only at COMMIT.

choices.text: Each stays closed from its ALTER until the COMMIT, after the slow rewrite and everything else
choices.why: Right. One transaction is one long lock on everything it touched.

choices.text: Nothing: they are different tables
choices.why: They wait for nothing of the first table, but their own locks last until the end of the shared transaction.

choices.text: PostgreSQL commits each ALTER automatically, as MySQL does
choices.why: That is MySQL's behaviour. PostgreSQL's DDL is transactional, as the ROLLBACK showed.

prompt: Right after `ADD CONSTRAINT total_positive CHECK (total_cents > 0) NOT VALID`, an insert with total_cents = 0 is tried. What happens?
hint: NOT VALID is about the rows already there.

choices.text: It is accepted until the constraint is validated
choices.why: That is the common misreading of NOT VALID. Only the existing rows are unchecked.

choices.text: It waits for VALIDATE CONSTRAINT to run
choices.why: Nothing waits; the insert was refused in about a millisecond.

choices.text: It is accepted with a warning
choices.why: A check constraint never warns; it refuses or accepts.

choices.text: It is refused
choices.why: Right. A NOT VALID constraint is enforced for new rows from the moment it is added.

prompt: While `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` held its lock in an open transaction, another session ran an UPDATE on the same table. What happened to the UPDATE?
hint: Which lock did pg_locks show for VALIDATE?

choices.text: It waited for the COMMIT
choices.why: It would have under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. VALIDATE takes SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE.

choices.text: It failed, because the table was being validated
choices.why: It returned UPDATE 1.

choices.text: It ran, but its row was not checked against the constraint
choices.why: Every new row version is checked by the constraint, validated or not.

choices.text: It ran at once, because SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE does not conflict with writes
choices.why: Right. Its time was the scan for id 2, not a wait.

prompt: Put the steps that gave orders_live a primary key without a long ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock in order.
hint: The index first; the NOT NULL proof before the key.
items: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_live_id ON orders_live (id)
ADD CONSTRAINT id_not_null CHECK (id IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID
ADD CONSTRAINT orders_live_pkey PRIMARY KEY USING INDEX orders_live_id
trap: Dropping the check before the key exists throws away the proof that lets the key skip its scan.

prompt: A migration tool runs every step inside BEGIN … COMMIT. A developer adds `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` to a migration. What happens?
hint: One of the two cautions at the end of the section.

choices.text: It is refused: no CONCURRENTLY inside a transaction block
choices.why: Right. The tool has to be told to run that step outside a transaction.

choices.text: It runs, but without CONCURRENTLY
choices.why: PostgreSQL never quietly drops the word; it refuses the statement.

choices.text: It builds an INVALID index that the tool then validates
choices.why: An INVALID index is what a failure halfway leaves; there is no validating it, only dropping and rebuilding.

choices.text: It works and holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE until COMMIT
choices.why: It does not get as far as taking a lock.

prompt: Put the phases of changing total_cents from integer to bigint in order.
hint: Four names: expand, backfill, switch, contract.
items: Add total_cents_new and a trigger that fills it on every write
Copy the old rows across in batches, committing each
Rename the columns and drop the trigger in one short transaction
trap: Backfilling before the trigger exists leaves every row written during the backfill without a value.

prompt: Why does backfill_total_cents commit after each batch instead of running one UPDATE over the whole table?
hint: What does a single huge transaction hold, and for how long?

choices.text: Because a procedure cannot update more than 100,000 rows at once
choices.why: There is no such limit; 100,000 was the batch the lesson chose.

choices.text: Because the trigger only fires on committed rows
choices.why: A trigger fires inside the statement, committed or not.

choices.text: So no transaction locks many rows for long or holds back VACUUM
choices.why: Right. Each batch is a short transaction, and the dead rows it leaves can be cleaned as it goes.

choices.text: To make the backfill faster overall
choices.why: Batches are usually a little slower overall. They are kinder, not faster.

prompt: How many batches did CALL backfill_total_cents(100000) commit on orders_live?
hint: Count the NOTICE lines.

prompt: The check after the backfill uses `IS DISTINCT FROM` rather than `<>`. What would `WHERE total_cents_new <> total_cents` have missed?
hint: What is NULL <> 5?

choices.text: Rows where the two values differ by more than an integer can hold
choices.why: <> compares a bigint and an integer correctly. The gap is NULL.

choices.text: Rows the trigger wrote during the backfill
choices.why: Those have equal values, and both operators count them as equal.

choices.text: Rows where total_cents_new is still NULL
choices.why: Right. NULL <> 5 is NULL, not true, so the row would not be counted.

choices.text: Nothing: the two are the same for numbers
choices.why: They are the same for two non-null numbers. With a NULL they differ.

prompt: You must add `CHECK (status IN ('paid', 'shipped', 'cancelled'))` to a 300-million-row table that is written all day. Which plan follows this lesson?
hint: Two statements, each under a different lock.

choices.text: ADD CONSTRAINT at night, when traffic is low
choices.why: It still scans 300 million rows under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE; low traffic only means fewer people queue.

choices.text: Add a new column with the check, backfill it, and switch
choices.why: Expand and contract is for changes that cannot be made cheap. A check can.

choices.text: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on status first, so that validating the check can use the index instead of the table
choices.why: Validating a check reads every row; no index makes that unnecessary.

choices.text: ADD CONSTRAINT … NOT VALID with a lock_timeout, then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT
choices.why: Right. A brief strong lock, bounded by the timeout, then a long scan that lets writes continue.

prompt: A retry script has failed five times in a row, each time with `canceling statement due to lock timeout`. What is the right next step?
hint: What does five failures in a row say about the table?

choices.text: Raise lock_timeout to five minutes and run it once more
choices.why: That turns the next attempt into exactly the outage the timeout was there to prevent.

choices.text: Look in pg_stat_activity for what has held the table so long
choices.why: Right. Something holds it for long periods, and that is the problem to solve first.

choices.text: Run the ALTER without lock_timeout, since the retries proved it is safe
choices.why: The retries proved the opposite: the lock is not free.

choices.text: Restart PostgreSQL to clear the locks
choices.why: A restart ends every session, which is a worse outage than the one being avoided.

prompt: A table's `email` column is `varchar(100)` and must become `varchar(255)`. Which approach is enough?
hint: Can a larger limit make any existing row invalid?

choices.text: Expand and contract: a new column, a backfill and a switch
choices.why: That is a lot of work for a change PostgreSQL makes by editing the catalogue.

choices.text: NOT VALID and VALIDATE, as for a check
choices.why: A type change has no NOT VALID form, and this one needs no check of the rows anyway.

choices.text: Wait for a maintenance window, because every type change rewrites the table
choices.why: Not every type change rewrites; the lesson measured this exact kind as instant.

choices.text: A plain ALTER COLUMN TYPE varchar(255), with lock_timeout
choices.why: Right. Raising the limit is instant, like varchar(20) to varchar(40); the timeout handles the queue.

prompt: Which of these keep the ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for only a moment on a large table? Choose all that apply.
hint: Catalogue edits versus anything that reads or writes every row.

choices.text: ADD COLUMN with a constant default
choices.why: Yes, since PostgreSQL 11.

choices.text: RENAME COLUMN
choices.why: Yes. A catalogue edit, which is why the switch was quick.

choices.text: ADD CONSTRAINT … CHECK … NOT VALID
choices.why: Yes. The existing rows are not read.

choices.text: ALTER COLUMN … TYPE bigint, from integer
choices.why: A rewrite, under the lock throughout.

choices.text: ADD COLUMN … DEFAULT gen_random_uuid()
choices.why: A volatile default rewrites the table.

prompt: `SET NOT NULL` skips its scan of the table when a valid ___ constraint already proves the column has no nulls.
hint: The kind added NOT VALID and then validated.
